correctness.rationale: Rotate each directed prime three-cycle so its least vertex p is first. For p<=349 all q>p are prime factors of p²−p+1, and all r>p, r≠q are prime factors of q²−q+1. Exact complete trial division enumerates every possibility without bounding the other two primes; all 70 two-edge candidates are archived in paths.csv and recomputed by verify.py, with exactly one closing path (349,121453,9710803). Independently checked by a second exact factorization calculation. Trial-division primality and F(349)=121453, F(121453)=7²·31·9710803, 349|F(9710803) establish the cycle. For squarefree N the divisor identity H(N)=∏F(p)/p and exact multiplication yield N=411612748708891 and H(N)=410433300314317. The finite cutoff follows because all cycles with minimum <=349 are enumerated; nothing is inferred about larger minima.

originality.rationale: Primary literature gives the reciprocal-gcd divisor identity and introduces cycles of sixth-cyclotomic prime factors but no exact minimum prime for a directed three-cycle or the specific 349→121453→9710803 witness. Complete primary-source and OEIS inspections, direct published Φ3 prime-pair result inspection, targeted scholarly searches and all nine actual published-finding corpus semantic searches identify no statement or stronger theorem implying the bounded cutoff. A reciprocal-pair condition concerns length-two mutual divisibility, not directed length-three cycles; similarity alone is not implication. Non-detection is not uniqueness proof, and an unindexed computation is an explicit residual risk.

value.rationale: The motivating paper explicitly studies and questions prime-factor cycles for the reciprocal-gcd-integrality construction. A directed prime three-cycle is the smallest length not excluded by reciprocal-pair obstructions. The exact least-vertex threshold 349, unique endpoint orbit, and first explicit 3-prime squarefree witness of this construction address a natural structural and computational question, provide a new concrete smaller-support phenomenon than the four-prime example, and may guide subsequent searches without requiring an infinite theorem.
